comments.body:
We recently merged a refactor to `develop` that enables clang-tidy's `readability-identifier-naming`. Your branch now has heavy conflicts that are largely mechanical. Below is a workflow that aligns your branch's naming with develop _before_ merging, which should minimize the merge conflicts.

## One-time setup

If you don't already have clang-tidy working in your env, on macOS:

```bash
brew install llvm@21
# Follow brew's hint to put $(brew --prefix llvm@21)/bin on PATH so run-clang-tidy is found.
```

## Workflow on your branch (before merging develop)

**1. Grab the new `.clang-tidy` from develop without pulling anything else.** Sync your fork on GitHub first, then:

```bash
git remote -v   # should show 'upstream' among others; if not:
# git remote set-url upstream git@github.com:XRPLF/rippled.git
git fetch upstream
git checkout upstream/develop -- .clang-tidy
```

**2. Reconfigure conan/cmake so `compile_commands.json` is fresh.**

**3. Apply renames for the files modified in your PR:**

```bash
git diff --name-only $(git merge-base HEAD upstream/develop) HEAD \
  | grep -E '\.(cpp|h|hpp|ipp)$' \
  | xargs run-clang-tidy -p build -fix -allow-no-checks
# or -p .build, or whatever your build dir is called
```

**4. Build + test, then commit as a single dedicated commit:**

```bash
cmake --build build -j8
git commit -am "refactor: Align identifier naming with develop"
```

**5. Now merge develop:**

```bash
git merge upstream/develop
```

## Extra

Run clang-tidy once more after the merge to catch any stragglers introduced from develop's side:

```bash
run-clang-tidy -p build -fix -allow-no-checks src tests
# or -p .build, or whatever your build dir is called
```

reviewCommentsList.author: Copilot
reviewCommentsList.body:
`operator+` for IOU STAmounts now default-constructs `STAmount x{}` and then assigns an `IOUAmount` into it. A default-constructed `STAmount` is native/integral, so the private `operator=(IOUAmount)` assertion (`integral() == false`) will fail in debug builds and can leave the returned amount with the wrong asset in release. Construct the result using `v1` (or at least `v1.asset()` / `v1.getFName()`) before assigning the IOU sum so the returned value preserves the correct Issue/Asset type.
```suggestion
    STAmount x{v1};
```

reviewCommentsList.author: Copilot
reviewCommentsList.body: In `canonicalize()` for integral amounts, `Number num(mIsNegative ? -mValue : mValue, ...)` negates `mValue` (a `std::uint64_t`) when negative, which underflows/wraps and then converts to a signed `Number::rep`. That can yield an implementation-defined/incorrect mantissa for negative values. Build the `Number` using a signed mantissa (with an explicit `std::int64_t` cast) or use the existing `Number(bool negative, internalrep mantissa, int exponent, unchecked)` ctor to avoid unsigned wraparound.

reviewCommentsList.author: Copilot
reviewCommentsList.body: `NumberSO` (and the global switchover setters) are removed here, but there are still call sites in the tree (e.g. `src/libxrpl/tx/apply.cpp` and `src/libxrpl/tx/applySteps.cpp`) that instantiate `NumberSO`. As-is, this change will break compilation; either update those remaining call sites in this PR or provide a replacement mechanism.

## High Level Overview of Change

    Use Number for IOUAmount and STAmount arithmetic
    
    * Guarded by amendment fixUniversalNumber
    * Produces slightly better accuracy in some computations.

### Context of Change

There are two many decimal floating point classes in rippled, and AMM needed a third.  This merges common code.  A side effect is that some transaction arithmetic becomes more accurate in the final digit or two.  Therefore this change is guarded by an amendment.

The first many commits introduce `Number`.  Only the final commit merges the common code with `IOUAmount` and `STAmount`, and introduces the amendment.

reviewCommentsList.body:
Yes, both by theory and testing.

Theory:  The Newton algorithm will reliably point towards the right answer.  If that right answer is between two representable values, and the starting guess is one of those representable values, then the algorithm either gives back the same answer, or the other representable value closest to the exact answer.  It never "wanders" away.

Practice:  The set up to this look reduces the domain to [1, 10).  Very significant testing was done throughout this small finite range, especially near the endpoints, and at the point where the difference between the initial guess and the exact answer is at a maximum.

I also tried going with a fixed number of iterations.  However testing revealed that the required number of iterations varied enough that I felt it was too expensive to hard code the maximum number of iterations when many inputs in the range [1, 10) required fewer than the maximum.

In the end, among these four approaches:

1.  Hard code the number of iterations:  Rejected because there was no one number of iterations that was acceptable.
2. Stop when r == rm1.  Rejected because the loop sometimes did not terminate because the algorithm would bounce between two values.
3. Stop when r == rm1 || r == rm2.  Accepted as the highest performance alternative while maintaining correctness.
4. Stop when r == rm1 || r == rm2 || r == rm3.  Although correct, a history of three values was never observed to be needed.  Rejected.

I want the `Number(rep mantissa)` constructor to be an implicit conversion from `rep` to `Number` and the `Number(rep mantissa, int exponent)` constructor to be marked `explicit`.

`Number` has a design such that conversions _from_ arithmetic, XRPAmount and IOUAmount are implicit, whereas conversions going the other way are explicit.  This facilitates "mixed-mode" arithmetic, with everything unambiguously converting to `Number`, which can represent the union of all values.  The resulting code is relatively clean.

However such a nicety is not warranted for the expression `{5, 3}`.  This expression is already not as "natural" and could mean several things.  Thus if this is supposed to be a `Number`, `Number{5, 3}` is required as the syntax.

reviews.author: intelliot
reviews.body:
This is a follow-up to #4192.

Rationale:

For most amendments, it is preferable to keep the default vote at `no` for the 1st release that understands the amendment, because the amendment's activation would amendment-block all current servers. If the amendment activates before the next release, then nodes could be amendment blocked even when they are only 1 release behind latest.

The default vote can be toggled to `yes` in a subsequent release. This has the effect of making it more likely that node operators have more lead time in order to review the changes and update their rippled software versions. Nodes would not get amendment blocked unless they are 2 releases behind.
